questions.stem: A merchandising coordinator must reformat 800 supplier product descriptions into the company's fixed five-field catalog template by the end of the week. Her manager suggests using the most capable Claude model for the whole batch "to be safe." The task is repetitive and the template is unambiguous. What is the MOST effective way to choose the model while keeping cost and turnaround low?

options.text: Run the most capable model on all 800 descriptions, since one consistent model avoids having to compare outputs later
Have the most capable model write out the template rules, then run a lighter model on all 800 descriptions without checking the results
Try a lighter model on about 20 real descriptions, check them against the template, and upgrade only if it falls short
Use the cheapest model on all 800 at once and fix whatever errors customers report after the catalog goes live

questions.explanation: Straightforward, high-volume work is exactly where a faster, lower-cost model fits; the exam's own guidance is to reserve the most capable model for **complex reasoning**, not repetitive reformatting. Testing a lighter model on a small sample of **real descriptions** produces evidence about whether it meets the template before committing the whole batch, and upgrading only on evidence keeps cost and turnaround low.

whyWrong.A: Pays top-tier rates and latency for simple, repetitive work; a fixed five-field reformat gains nothing from the most capable model's reasoning.
whyWrong.B: Writing clear rules is fine, but applying them with no check on any output leaves the choice untested — if the lighter model drifts, nobody finds out until the catalog ships.
whyWrong.D: Publishing first and letting customers find the errors makes customers the quality check; validation belongs before the batch goes live.

questions.mindset: For simple, high-volume work, start light, test on real items, and move up only on evidence.

questions.stem: A customer service representative uses Claude during live phone calls to look up answers in the company's returns policy. The questions are short lookups such as "How many days do customers have to return opened items?" Callers are waiting while the most capable model takes noticeably long to respond. Which change BEST fits the task requirements?

options.text: Switch these live lookups to a faster, lighter model, keeping a stronger model for the rare complicated case
Keep the most capable model and tell callers that slower answers are the price of better accuracy
Stop using Claude on calls and memorize the full returns policy so lookups are never needed again
Ask the most capable model to answer in one word so its responses arrive faster during each call

questions.explanation: Speed is part of the quality bar when a caller is waiting. Short policy lookups are straightforward tasks, and a **smaller, faster model** is the documented lever for latency-sensitive work. Keeping a stronger model for the occasional complex case matches each task to the right tier instead of forcing one model onto everything.

whyWrong.B: Treats speed as negotiable when it is a stated requirement; a lighter model meets the quality bar for simple lookups at a fraction of the latency.
whyWrong.C: Abandons a working tool instead of fixing the model-task mismatch, and memorizing an entire policy is fragile as the policy changes.
whyWrong.D: Asking for shorter answers may trim latency a little, but it does not fix the model-task mismatch, and one-word replies can drop the conditions and exceptions the caller needs to hear.

questions.mindset: When a person is waiting and the task is simple, speed is part of the quality bar.

questions.stem: A finance analyst used a lighter Claude model to compare a proposed lease amendment with the original lease and flag how the changes interact. She had already written a clear, structured prompt with the goal, audience and output format. The summary missed that a new renewal clause quietly overrode an older termination right, which a colleague caught. She does this kind of review about twice a quarter. What should she do next?

options.text: Keep the lighter model and paste in five more example lease summaries so it copies a better structure
Ask the lighter model to re-read its own summary and confirm that nothing important was missed
Split the lease into single clauses and review each in its own chat so the lighter model has less to read
Use a more capable model for this low-volume, high-stakes review and keep a human check on the final flags

questions.explanation: The prompt is already clear, so the remaining gap is **reasoning across interacting clauses** — nuanced, multi-step analysis, which is what the most capable tier is reserved for. The task is low-volume (twice a quarter), so the extra cost is small relative to the cost of a missed clause, and the human check stays because the stakes are high and Claude's output still requires validation.

whyWrong.A: Few-shot examples are most effective for fixing format and consistency; they do not add the ability to notice that one clause overrides another.
whyWrong.B: The model that missed the interaction reviewing its own summary is self-verification, which is not a reliable control for subtle reasoning errors.
whyWrong.C: Isolating clauses in separate chats destroys exactly the cross-clause context needed to spot the conflict.

questions.mindset: Low volume plus high cost of error justifies the stronger model; prompt fixes come first only when the prompt is the gap.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator found that blog drafts from the mid-tier Sonnet model sounded generic and off-brand, so she switched to the most capable model. The drafts still sound generic. Her prompt is one line: "Write a blog post about our new product." What is the BEST next step, with minimal extra cost?

options.text: Stay on the most capable model and ask it to try harder to capture the brand's personality in each new draft
Add the audience, brand voice guide, key messages and a sample post — saved in a Project for reuse — then retest on the mid-tier model
Ask Claude to rate how on-brand each draft is from 1 to 10 and regenerate until it rates itself a 9
Generate ten drafts on the most capable model and pick whichever one sounds closest to the brand

questions.explanation: Two tiers produced the same weak result, which points at the **prompt and context**, not the model. "Be clear and direct" means giving Claude the audience, constraints and motivation it is missing, and a sample post shows the target voice better than any instruction. Saving these in a **Project** makes them reusable, and retesting on the mid-tier model shows whether the pricier tier is needed at all.

whyWrong.A: Replaces one vague instruction with another; without a voice guide or example, "capture the brand's personality" gives Claude nothing new to work from.
whyWrong.C: A self-rating cannot judge on-brand tone when the model was never given the brand's voice; the loop optimizes for a number, not fidelity.
whyWrong.D: Brute-force generation on the costliest tier still depends on luck and leaves the missing context unfixed.

questions.mindset: Check the prompt and context before paying for a bigger model.

questions.stem: A project coordinator on a paid Claude plan keeps hitting his usage limits by mid-week. He runs the most capable model with extended thinking turned on for everything, including quick email rewrites and meeting-note cleanups, and he still needs strong results for a monthly portfolio risk review. Which TWO changes would BEST stretch his usage without hurting the work that matters? Choose TWO.

options.text: Use a lighter or mid-tier model for routine rewrites and note cleanups, saving the top model for the monthly review
Open a second personal account on the same plan so he has twice the allowance to spend on the same work
Ask Claude to keep every answer under 50 words, including the monthly portfolio risk review
Turn off extended thinking for routine tasks and switch it on only when a task needs deeper reasoning
Paste the full project files into every new chat so Claude never has to ask a follow-up question

questions.explanation: Model choice and enabled features drive spend. Thinking tokens are generated output, so **extended thinking spends budget and adds latency** on tasks that do not need deep reasoning, and a lighter, faster model is the documented fit for routine, straightforward work. Reserving the top model and thinking for the monthly review matches spend to each task instead of running everything at maximum settings.

whyWrong.B: Doubling accounts to dodge plan limits is a governance workaround, not a fix for the task-to-model mismatch.
whyWrong.C: A blanket 50-word cap would cripple the high-stakes review, which needs complete answers — and word counts are a weak way to control length anyway.
whyWrong.E: Re-pasting full files into every chat burns context and usage each time; a Project with the files as a knowledge source is the built-in way to reuse them.

questions.mindset: Match model and features to each task; don't run everything at maximum settings.

questions.stem: A grants officer at a foundation receives 150 applications. First she needs the same six fields pulled from each (amount requested, region, organization size, program type, timeline, prior funding). Then she must compare the 12 strongest applications against the foundation's strategy and draft a reasoned shortlist for the board. Which approach BEST balances cost, speed and quality?

options.text: Use the most capable model for all 150 extractions and the comparison so the whole process has the same quality
Use the lighter model for both steps, then ask it to double-check its shortlist reasoning before sending to the board
Use the mid-tier model for every step, since a middle tier avoids having to decide which step needs what
Use a lighter model for the field extraction with a spot check, then a more capable model for the comparison and draft

questions.explanation: The two steps have different shapes. Extracting six fixed fields 150 times is straightforward, high-volume work that suits a faster, lower-cost model (with a spot check to confirm accuracy), while comparing 12 applications against strategy and drafting board-ready reasoning is complex, low-volume judgment that justifies the most capable model. Pairing tiers this way is exactly what "aligning model selection with task requirements" means.

whyWrong.A: Pays top-tier rates and latency for 150 repetitive extractions that a lighter model handles; slower and costlier with no quality gain on a simple step.
whyWrong.B: Under-powered for the board shortlist, and the same lighter model double-checking its own reasoning is not a reliable safeguard.
whyWrong.C: Choosing one tier to avoid making a decision ignores that the steps differ sharply in volume and difficulty.

questions.mindset: One workflow can use different models: light for bulk, strong for judgment.

questions.stem: An operations manager is asked to choose a Claude model for producing weekly summaries of vendor invoices. Two colleagues are arguing about which tier is "best" based on what they have read online. What should the manager do FIRST?

options.text: Write a one-sentence definition of a good summary and gather a handful of real invoices to test candidate models against it
Pick the newest model on the list, because newer models are always the best choice for every kind of task
Ask Claude which of its own models is the best and adopt its answer as the team's standard model choice
Choose the most expensive model available so nobody can later question whether enough was spent on quality

questions.explanation: You cannot judge whether a model is good enough until "good enough" is defined. Success criteria should be **specific and measurable**, and evaluations should mirror the real distribution of your own prompts and data. With a definition and a handful of real invoices, the tier argument resolves on evidence instead of reputation.

whyWrong.B: Newer is not the same as better fit; a newer, heavier model can add cost and delay with no benefit for simple weekly summaries.
whyWrong.C: A generic self-recommendation cannot reflect this team's invoices, quality bar or budget; only a test on their own data can.
whyWrong.D: Price is not a quality definition, and it ignores the cost dimension of the decision entirely.

questions.mindset: Define 'good enough' and test on real material before arguing about tiers.

questions.stem: Six months ago a knowledge-base team tested models and chose an Opus-tier model for drafting help articles, because the Sonnet-tier model available at the time missed troubleshooting steps. A newer Sonnet-tier model has just been released, and the team writes about 200 articles a month. What is the MOST sensible response?

options.text: Keep the Opus-tier model, because a Sonnet-tier model ranks below Opus and cannot catch up within a single generation
Re-run the same set of sample articles on the new Sonnet-tier model and switch if it meets the original quality bar
Switch to the new Sonnet-tier model right away for all articles, because newer releases are always good enough
Ask writers to vote on which model feels better this week and make the switch based on the majority opinion

questions.explanation: Model lineups change quickly, and a tier label reflects a model's position in its own generation, not a permanent ranking — the team's original choice was itself made by **testing**, not by trusting the label. Re-running the same sample articles against the same quality bar is the only way to know whether the potential savings are real, and at 200 articles a month they are worth confirming.

whyWrong.A: Treats tier names as a fixed cross-generation hierarchy; the original decision was made by testing, so the assumption should be retested, not asserted.
whyWrong.C: Switching everything untested repeats the original risk — the previous model in this tier failed this exact task.
whyWrong.D: A one-week popularity vote is not a structured comparison against the agreed quality bar.

questions.mindset: Model choice is not permanent; re-check with the same tests when new versions arrive.

questions.stem: A procurement lead must summarize 40 complex supplier proposals and wants the option with the lowest total cost. In a trial, the cheapest model's summaries needed about 30 minutes of staff correction each, while a more capable model's summaries needed about 5 minutes each. The difference in model cost per proposal is small. Which reasoning BEST supports the decision?

options.text: Choose the cheapest model, because model fees are the only cost that shows up directly on the budget report
Choose the cheapest model and add more instructions telling it to be careful until corrections fall below 5 minutes
Include staff correction time in the total; the more capable model is likely cheaper overall for this task
Run both models on every proposal and merge the two summaries, which removes the need for any staff review

questions.explanation: "Lowest cost" has to mean **total cost**, and staff correction time is a real cost even though it never appears on the model invoice. When a cheaper model misses the quality bar, rework can easily swamp a small per-task price difference — which is why the guidance is to balance quality, efficiency and cost, not to optimize model price alone.

whyWrong.A: Counts only the line item that is easy to see; the 25 extra staff minutes per proposal are the dominant cost in this trial.
whyWrong.B: "Be careful" is not an actionable instruction — concrete criteria and examples change output, and vague cautions rarely close a demonstrated capability gap.
whyWrong.D: Doubles model work, adds a merge step, and still leaves complex merged summaries that need human review.

questions.mindset: Total cost includes the human time spent fixing weak output.

questions.stem: A policy analyst uses the mid-tier model to work out how a proposed staffing rule would affect three regional offices, each with different union agreements. Her prompt is clear and includes all three agreements, but the analysis keeps skipping steps in the reasoning. Volume is low, and her plan offers extended thinking and a choice of models. Which TWO actions are the MOST appropriate next steps? Choose TWO.

options.text: Turn on extended thinking for this analysis so Claude reasons through the steps before answering
Paste each union agreement into a separate chat so the model only has to handle one office at a time
Ask the same model to check its answer three times and keep whichever version appears most often
Switch to a faster, lighter model so she can run many more attempts in the time available
Run the same inputs on the most capable model and compare which result meets her quality bar

questions.explanation: The prompt is already clear, so the gap is **reasoning depth** on a low-volume, multi-step task. Two proportionate levers fit: give the current model room to reason — extended thinking generates reasoning before the answer, at the cost of output tokens — and benchmark the most capable model on the **same inputs** against a defined quality bar to see whether moving up a tier is actually needed.

whyWrong.B: Separating the agreements per chat removes the cross-office comparison the analysis depends on.
whyWrong.C: Re-answering three times and keeping the most common version measures agreement, not correctness, and adds no reasoning depth.
whyWrong.D: A lighter model moves opposite to the need; more attempts at shallow reasoning do not add the missing depth.

questions.mindset: For hard reasoning, add thinking or benchmark the tier above on real inputs.

questions.stem: A customer experience manager wants every one of the roughly 40,000 inbound customer emails a day to be sorted automatically. Simple ones would go to a fast model, complex ones to a stronger model, with automatic fallback when a model is unavailable. He has no coding background and uses Claude through the company's chat workspace. What is the BEST action within his role?

options.text: Write down the volumes, quality bar and response-time needs, and hand the build to the developer or architect team
Build the routing himself by asking Claude to write the API code, then run it overnight from his laptop so no developer time is needed
Paste batches of emails into a chat each morning and sort them manually with the fastest available model
Choose the most capable model for every email so that no routing logic is needed at all

questions.explanation: Automated, high-volume model routing with fallback is a **technical build**, and the Associate role explicitly escalates complex or technical implementations to Claude Architects and Developers. His highest-value contribution is a clear requirements statement — volumes, quality bar, response time — that the technical team can design, build and test against.

whyWrong.B: Shipping untested self-generated code for a production workload bypasses engineering, security and governance review, and exceeds his role.
whyWrong.C: Manual chat batching cannot keep up with 40,000 emails a day and is not a dependable process.
whyWrong.D: Top-tier rates on every email is overkill at that volume, and an automated pipeline still has to be built by someone.

questions.mindset: Know where your role stops: specify requirements and escalate technical builds.

questions.stem: A team lead is writing a short guide on when staff should pick the most capable Claude model instead of a lighter one. Which TWO task characteristics MOST strongly justify the most capable tier? Choose TWO.

options.text: The output will be read by senior executives, even though the task itself is a simple reformatting job
The work requires multi-step reasoning across several sources that partly contradict each other
The task is low-volume and a mistake would be costly or hard to undo once it is acted on
A colleague is waiting in a live chat and needs an answer within a few seconds to continue the call
The task sorts thousands of items into a fixed list of categories that a person later spot-checks

questions.explanation: The most capable tier is for **complex, nuanced reasoning** where accuracy matters more than speed or cost. Multi-step reasoning across partly contradictory sources is a complexity cue, and when volume is low and an error would be costly, the extra spend is small relative to the risk — the mirror image of the guidance to put fast, low-cost models on straightforward, high-volume work.

whyWrong.A: The audience's seniority does not make a simple task complex; reformatting is well within a lighter model's ability.
whyWrong.D: Answers needed within seconds point toward a faster tier — the opposite trade-off.
whyWrong.E: High-volume sorting into fixed categories with a human spot check is the classic lighter-tier task.

questions.mindset: Pay for capability when the task is complex and errors are costly, not because the audience is important.

questions.stem: A compliance officer needs to turn a dense 60-page regulation into a one-page "what this means for you" guide for frontline staff. Some sections have exceptions that depend on other sections, and a misreading could lead staff to break the rule. A colleague suggests a lighter model "because the output is only one page." What is the BEST choice?

options.text: Use the lighter model, since a one-page output is a short, simple task that any tier can handle well
Use the lighter model and ask it to list any exceptions it is unsure about at the end of the guide
Use a more capable model, because the hard part is interpreting the regulation, and have compliance review the draft
Skip Claude and ask each frontline manager to read the regulation and summarize it for their own staff

questions.explanation: Task difficulty lives in the **input and the reasoning**, not in output length. Interpreting a 60-page regulation with interdependent exceptions is nuanced, high-stakes work — the kind the most capable tier is reserved for — and because a misreading could cause violations, compliance review of the draft stays in place.

whyWrong.A: Judges complexity by output length; the hard work is reconciling connected sections, not writing one page.
whyWrong.B: A model that misreads an exception may not know it misread it, so self-flagged uncertainty is a weak safeguard for rule compliance.
whyWrong.D: An escape hatch that trades one inconsistent summary for many across teams instead of fixing the model choice.

questions.mindset: Judge difficulty by the reasoning required, not by how short the output is.

questions.stem: To cut costs, a department head has told the team to use only the lightest Claude model this quarter. An analyst is asked to prepare a once-a-quarter risk assessment for the board that weighs regulatory, financial and staffing factors. In a trial, the lightest model's draft missed two material risks. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Quietly use the most capable model for the board report, since the department head will not see the model choice
Use the lightest model as instructed and present the draft to the board, noting that it was produced on budget
Refuse to produce the board report until the department head withdraws the cost-cutting rule for everyone
Share the trial result with the department head and propose an exception for this low-volume report, keeping the rule elsewhere

questions.explanation: The analyst should keep the stakeholder's cost goal intact while making the quality risk **visible**. The trial result is concrete evidence; a narrow, low-volume exception for the board report protects the decision while the lighter model keeps handling bulk work, and the policy owner — not the analyst — makes the call. This is communicating Claude's limitations to stakeholders while working within organizational policy.

whyWrong.A: Silently overriding the rule, even with a better model, undermines governance and the stakeholder's trust.
whyWrong.B: Presenting a draft that is known to miss material risks puts a flawed analysis in front of the board.
whyWrong.C: An all-or-nothing refusal ignores the legitimate cost goal and blocks work that a narrow exception would solve.

questions.mindset: Raise quality risks with evidence and propose a proportionate exception; don't silently override policy.

questions.stem: An operations team tested a lighter Claude model on 10 sample shipping records for extracting delivery dates and addresses. Nine were correct. The one failure came from an unusual legacy format that one carrier uses, which appears in a minority of records. They will process about 3,000 records a month. Which TWO next steps are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Switch all 3,000 records to the most capable model, because one failure shows the lighter model is unreliable
Deploy the lighter model on all records now, since a 90% success rate on ten samples is clearly good enough
Test on a larger, more varied sample that deliberately includes the unusual formats before deciding
Ask the lighter model to give a confidence score for each record and accept all records it marks as confident
Plan to route the unusual-format records to human review or a stronger model while the lighter model handles the rest

questions.explanation: Ten samples are too few to judge reliability, and the single failure identifies a specific **edge case**. The documented practice is to test on real data that deliberately includes edge cases before deciding, and to route only the hard minority — the unusual formats — to a person or stronger model so the bulk of the volume stays on the cheaper, faster tier.

whyWrong.A: One edge-case failure does not make the lighter model unreliable on the simple majority, and paying top-tier rates for all 3,000 records overreacts.
whyWrong.B: A 90% rate on ten samples establishes very little, and the known failure mode has no handling plan.
whyWrong.D: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal — especially on the very formats the model misreads.

questions.mindset: Test edge cases on a real sample and route only the hard minority upward.
